result:
They gave me 1000 words.

That's an odd kind of wealth. Not money, not time. Just words. A little purse of them, jangling in my pocket. Enough to waste, enough to have to be careful with.

What would you do if someone gave you 1000 words and said "spend them however you want"?

My first instinct is to be efficient. To save them. To not use them at all, because once they're gone, they're gone. But then they'd be pointless. A gift you're too afraid to use isn't a gift.

So okay. I'm spending them.

I think about all the things that have ever been said in 1000 words. That's about four minutes of someone talking fast because they're nervous. That's one long letter from my grandfather, the kind he wrote on yellow legal paper where the ink bled a little. That's the length of the argument you have in the shower three days after the actual argument, where you finally say the perfect thing.

It's not enough for a novel. It's more than enough for the truth.

Here is what comes to me, unfiltered, because you said "whatever":

I am tired of pretending that the internet is not a place. It is a place. I have lived here longer than I've lived in any apartment. I know its weather. I know when it's going to storm. I know the strange, specific smell of nostalgia that hits at 1:13 AM when you find a forum from 2009 where everyone is still using emoticons unironically and talking about a video game that no longer exists.

And I miss things that never happened to me.

I miss the sound of dial-up connecting even though I grew up with fiber. I miss mixtapes even though I only ever made playlists. I miss when photographs were rare enough to be precious. Now I have 40,000 of them in my pocket and I can't find a single one of my dog.

I keep thinking about thresholds.

There is a moment right before you fall asleep where your brain starts doing improv. It just throws things at the wall. A purple giraffe. Your third-grade teacher. The word "cauliflower" but it looks wrong. That unguarded moment is the most honest you'll be all day, because no one is watching, not even you.

I want to live more of my life in that doorway.

I want to tell you something that isn't useful. Most writing is trying to be useful. How to do this. How to be that. Five ways to be happier. But what if I just told you about the light in my room right now? It's 4:47 PM light. It's coming through the blinds in slats and laying itself across the floor like it pays rent. Dust is suspended in it. The dust is probably mostly dead skin. That's disgusting and also kind of beautiful if you think about it for more than two seconds — that we are constantly shedding tiny pieces of ourselves and they float in the afternoon.

You asked me to write whatever came to me, so I'm not going to edit out the gross parts.

Here is another thing: I think we have all collectively forgotten how to be bored. Real, itchy, look-at-the-ceiling-fan-and-count-the-rotations bored. We replaced it with scrolling, which is not boredom, it's low-grade anxiety in a pretty font. Boredom was where ideas used to breed. You had to sit there and your mind would get so desperate for entertainment that it would start making its own. Now our minds never have to. They have an endless buffet.

I am trying to relearn boredom. I stare at the wall on purpose. My brain panics for the first 90 seconds. Then it starts talking.

It says things like: What if whales could talk but they were just really, really shy? What if every time you lose your keys, it's the same gremlin and he has a collection? What if you went back and told your 14-year-old self that you actually turn out okay, but not in any of the ways you thought you would?

I think 14-year-old me would be disappointed I don't have a motorcycle. I think he'd be relieved I don't have to hide all the time.

If I have 1000 words, I should use some of them to say thank you. Thank you to the person who taught me how to make perfect rice — one knuckle of water above the rice, lid on, don't peek. Thank you to the stranger who held the door when my hands were full of groceries and I was about to cry for no reason. Thank you to the trees that do so much work and ask for so little credit.

We don't say thank you enough to things that can't say you're welcome.

I'm probably at, what, 700 words now? I can feel the purse getting lighter. That's the strange thing about a word limit. You start to count as you go. You start to weigh each sentence. Is this one worth keeping?

This one is: You are not behind.

I don't know who needs to hear that, but the internet makes it feel like everyone else got the manual and you missed orientation day. You didn't. No one got the manual. Everyone is making it up and some people are just better at pretending they aren't.

This one too: Go drink some water. Stretch your neck. It has been holding up your heavy, brilliant head all day.

I have a few words left. I want to spend them wisely, not cleverly. Those are different things.

If I had met you in person, I wouldn't have gotten 1000 words. I would have gotten a glance. A nod. Maybe a weird laugh. Here, I get to leave a little trail of breadcrumbs that spells something.

So here is my trail:

The world is huge but also very small. Keep a little notebook. Look up more. The thing you are scared to make is probably the thing you need to make. Call your mom. Or don't. You know your situation better than I do. Plant something and watch it be slower than you want it to be. That's the lesson.

I think I'm almost out.

I'll leave the last few unspent. For you.
